inputs.description: ISO8601 UTC start of the window around the alarm, e.g. 2026-09-03T12:00:00Z.
ISO8601 UTC end of the window, e.g. 2026-09-03T12:30:00Z.

What to inspect on the host if a live look is needed. One of: triage (default - load, top CPU/memory processes, disk, boot time), top_cpu, top_memory, disk_usage, memory_usage, network_connections, running_services, failed_services, recent_logins, shell_history, cron_jobs, recent_syslog, process_tree, boot_time, package_changes.
auto = only look inside the host when SSM history does not explain the spike (default, cheapest). always = always inspect. never = metrics and SSM history only.

params.command: aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name CPUUtilization --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value={{ Inputs.instance_id }} --start-time {{ Inputs.window_start }} --end-time {{ Inputs.window_end }} --period 60 --statistics Average Maximum --region {{ Inputs.region }} --output json
aws ssm list-commands --instance-id {{ Inputs.instance_id }} --max-results 50 --region {{ Inputs.region }} --output json

llm_description:
Investigates a CPU spike on an EC2 instance end to end and says what caused it.

First it correlates CloudWatch CPU with AWS SSM Run Command history, looking back 30 minutes before the spike, because the command that causes a spike always precedes it. If that identifies a likely cause it reports the exact command, when it ran and its comment, and stops there.

If SSM history does not explain the spike, it then inspects the host itself over SSM and returns live state: load, top CPU and memory consumers, disk, memory, network connections, services, logins, shell history, cron jobs and timers, system logs, or package changes — set host_action to choose, default 'triage'.

Use for any EC2 CPU alarm (for example *-cpu-high) or when asked what caused high CPU on an instance, whether someone ran something on a box, whether load was self-inflicted, or what process is consuming CPU. Needs the instance id and a time window around the alarm.

Set inspect_host=always to force the host look, or never to stay on metrics and SSM history only. Read-only throughout: it inspects, and never changes anything on the host.

Note: SSH sessions, cron jobs and boot-time processes leave no trace in SSM command history. An empty SSM result means nothing was run via SSM, not that nothing happened — the host inspection (shell_history, cron_jobs, recent_logins) covers that gap.
